courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching
md: 3DGS keeps NeRF's blending formula but replaces the implicit neural field with explicit primitives. Explicit primitives can be projected and rasterized, so rendering cost scales with the number of splats that touch a pixel, not with hundreds of network queries per ray.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: Portable C and C++ code does not get LL/SC semantics. `compare_exchange` is defined as a value comparison; on an LL/SC machine the compiler builds it from an LL/SC loop that starts *after* your earlier plain load of `top`. The window where ABA strikes (between that load and the CAS) is outside the reservation, so ABA is back.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: Shapley values are a summary, not a full account. They need $v$ for all $2^n$ configurations (16 here; for many components, sampled orders are the usual approximation). They hide that P is harmful without R, and they average over queries. Report the interaction cells and per-query spread too.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Missing function-level checks and privilege escalation
md: Every function has an owner question (which roles may call it) and every object has one (which users may touch it). A request must pass both. Hiding buttons and URLs answers neither.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: AD is a replicated database of identities and rules. DCs hold it, LDAP reads it, Kerberos and NTLM use it to sign people in, and GPOs push its settings to machines. Every attack in this course either steals proof of an identity or gains the right to write to this database.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Delegation: letting a server act as you, and how it goes wrong
md: Delegation lets a service obtain tickets as its users. Unconstrained trusts the server with users' TGTs; constrained trusts it with a list of back ends; RBCD lets the back end decide. Keep admins non-delegable, remove unconstrained delegation, and watch 4742 and 5136 for delegation changes.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Keep powerful credentials off weak machines: tier admin accounts, use PAWs, put admins in Protected Users, mark them non-delegable, rotate local admin passwords with LAPS and service passwords with gMSAs.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: JScript, VBScript and HTA: script hosts and their process trees
md: Node's documentation is blunt: 'The node:vm module is not a security mechanism. Do not use it to run untrusted code.' The fakes give visibility, not safety. Run emulation only inside the isolated analysis VM, exactly as you would run the sample itself.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Exploitation is a ladder of capabilities: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload. Every mitigation removes or weakens one rung, and the earlier the rung, the more bug-specific and costly the attacker's workaround.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Machine learning in one lesson: weights, loss and gradients
md: Lab rules for the whole course: run every attack only against models you train yourself, on your own machine. The same code aimed at someone else's deployed model or API is an attack on their system and needs written permission, like any other security test. Keep runs small: CPU, two threads (`OMP_NUM_THREADS=2`), one process at a time.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Broken defences: obfuscated gradients and adaptive attacks
md: Detectors and input transformations that "remove" adversarial noise have the worst track record. If a defence works by making the gradient useless instead of making the model right, an adaptive attacker who knows the defence will route around it. NIST's definition of white-box includes knowledge of the mitigations for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Model extraction: stealing a model through its API
md: Every answer an API gives is information about the model. Precision (full scores, logprobs) makes extraction cheap; volume makes any extraction possible. Control both, and watch accounts in aggregate, because large campaigns spread across many of them.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Running a purple team exercise
md: A purple team exercise is a loop per technique: context, expectation, execution, investigation, fix, retest, record. The output is not a list of what the red team achieved but a list of what the blue team can now see that it could not see in the morning.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
md: Treat the environment as part of the training algorithm. Its reward defines what is learned, its isolation defines what can be cheated, and its throughput (containers times 3600 divided by episode seconds) defines how many steps you can afford.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: The lethal trifecta and excessive agency
md: "Read-only" tools are not harmless in a trifecta. A tool that only fetches URLs is a perfect exit: the data goes out in the request.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: MCP and agent tools: when tool descriptions are the attack
md: Every MCP server you add is code you run and text your model obeys. Install few, from publishers you trust; pin and review their descriptions; show full arguments on approval; sandbox local servers; and do not combine private-data tools, untrusted-content tools and outbound tools in one agent.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
md: Each second-generation scheme buys one property with another: exact distributions with model-dependent tests or zero robustness gains, paraphrase robustness with slow rejection sampling, code detection with model access, user ids with more text, public verification with long outputs. Pick the property your use case cannot live without.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Validation is a fixed checklist the receiver owns: pinned algorithm, trusted issuer's key, signature, iss, aud, exp and nbf with small leeway, type. A library helps only when you pass it every one of those rules.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report. You will also meet BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model), which describes what real companies' programmes do rather than prescribing a target.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
md: Finding bugs is linear work; removing bug classes compounds. A mature programme spends part of its budget on defaults, paved roads and language choices that make the next thousand findings never happen.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes (4xx codes such as 400 Bad Request mean the request itself is wrong, so it fails the same way again), billing or quota errors.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
md: Forced periodic rotation makes passwords weaker, not stronger: people make the smallest possible change. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider (a cybercriminal group that targets companies through their IT help desks, lesson 12) repeats NIST's advice to refrain from recurring password changes. Change on evidence of compromise instead.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
md: Identity attacks leave traces in authentication logs: failures, travel, new devices, MFA changes. Centralising login through SSO makes those traces easy to collect, and makes the IdP the account to protect most.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Over-the-air updates: UN R156 and the Uptane framework
md: Split trust so that one stolen key is not enough: keys handled by people for *what is allowed to exist*, online keys for *who gets what*, and a version floor the online side cannot lower. Then make the car report what it runs.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a tiny BitNet and run it from packed bytes
md: The whole method fits on a laptop: a quantizer in the forward pass, an STE in the backward pass, then 2 bits per weight and integer adds at inference. The hard part in practice is the kernel, and matching training's quantizers exactly.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model
md: Misconception: "a sandbox escape is worse than a renderer bug, so it must be Critical." Chromium rates a renderer sandbox escape **High** because it needs the precondition of a compromised renderer. Critical is reserved for bugs that reach privileged code straight from a web page, or full chains.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Memory safety strategy: the Rule of 2, MiraclePtr, Rust and RLBox
md: Misconception: "a sandbox makes a memory bug harmless." It makes it worth less. A sandboxed decoder bug still gives code execution inside that sandbox, which is why Chromium still fixes and rewards such bugs as High, and why the Rule of 2 prefers removing the unsafe language when it can.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
md: LRU-K is not "keep the last K timestamps and you are done". Without a correlated reference period, a transaction that touches a page twice in a millisecond makes it look hot; without retained history, every page re-entering the pool starts at infinite distance and is evicted first.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Availability engineering: nines, redundancy and failure domains
md: Availability = uptime over total time. Hard dependencies multiply availabilities; independent redundant copies multiply failure rates; MTTR is a lever as strong as MTBF. Redundancy is only as good as its independence, so map failure domains, including software versions and admin identities.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
md: Assume production identity is lost. Give backups their own control plane, immutable and time-based retention, delayed and out-of-band-approved deletions, keys you cannot lose, alerts on every significant change, and restore into an isolated environment before anything returns to production.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
md: DORA requires a BIA, backup and restore procedures with segregated restore systems, yearly continuity and switchover tests, a crisis function, and TLPT on production every three years for designated firms. The UK sets impact tolerances per important business service and requires proof, by severe but plausible scenario tests, that firms stay within them.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost
md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Data races: pthreads in C versus Send and Sync in Rust
md: Data race: unsynchronized conflicting accesses, undefined behavior, ruled out at compile time by the borrow rules plus Send and Sync. Race condition: a timing-dependent logic bug, still possible, still memory safe.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Activation patching worked through: two directions and a shortcut
md: Denoising asks whether a component is enough to restore the behavior; noising asks whether the behavior needs it. AND-like circuits hide from denoising, OR-like backups hide from noising, and gradient shortcuts are trustworthy only for small patches.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
md: Nothing on facebook.com was vulnerable in that case. An extension with access to a site is effectively a trusted script on that site. For a site owner this risk sits outside your perimeter; for an organisation that manages its employees' browsers, it is squarely inside it.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Where the evidence lives when there is no server to seize
md: Cloud incident response reconstructs what identities did through the provider's API, across four evidence layers: control plane, data plane, workload and identity provider. What you can prove is decided before the incident, by which logs were on and where they were kept.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Identity incidents: tokens, consent grants and mailbox rules
md: Misconception: "we reset the password, so the attacker is out". A reset leaves forwarding rules, registered MFA methods, OAuth consent grants and app passwords in place, and already issued access tokens keep working for up to about an hour in apps without CAE. Disable, revoke, then hunt for each kind of persistence.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
md: Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
md: Common misconception: "we are on a big cloud, so the provider handles security." The provider secures its platform. Your identities, keys, data and configuration are yours, and even provider-side bugs usually ended with a customer to-do: regenerate keys after ChaosDB, update agents after OMIGOD.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Logging and detection: what key abuse looks like in CloudTrail
md: Log everything that changes configuration, keep it in a place attackers cannot reach, turn on data events for buckets that hold sensitive data, and alert on a short list of high-signal events: logging disabled, root use, new access keys and users, policy changes, and known credentials used from new places.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three things the silhouette cannot do. It is undefined for k = 1, so it can never tell you "this data has no clusters" (our k = 3 winner at 0.54 is not strong evidence of anything). It needs all pairwise distances, so it costs O(n squared) work. And it rewards compact well-separated blobs, so it is biased toward the kind of answer k-means produces, which makes it a poor referee between k-means and a density method.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules: rules about how the function's definition is shared between files. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: TSan must see **all** synchronization. Code not built with the flag (a prebuilt library, inline assembly) can cause false positives or missed races. That is why Rust's std should be rebuilt with the sanitizer via `-Zbuild-std`. The Rust unstable book also says Rust TSan does not support `std::sync::atomic::fence` or synchronization done in inline assembly, and rebuilding std does not change that.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Weaker but useful: sequential and causal consistency
md: Herlihy and Wing showed sequential consistency is **not local**: every object can be sequentially consistent while the system as a whole is not. Linearizability is local, which is one reason it composes better.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: SAT solvers: DPLL, unit propagation and clause learning
md: CDCL = DPLL + conflict analysis that learns a clause + backjumping to the level where the learned clause becomes unit and forces (asserts) its last literal + watched literals for cheap propagation + activity-based decisions and restarts. Each conflict teaches the solver something it never has to rediscover.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Pin by digest so you always run the same bytes; sign in CI and verify at admission so you only run bytes your pipeline produced.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: A pod's identity is its service account token plus whatever cloud role it can reach. Mount tokens only where needed, give each app its own service account, and map cloud access per service account instead of per node.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Escapes in the runtime: runc CVE-2019-5736 and Leaky Vessels
md: Runtime escapes come from the runtime briefly holding host resources while entering a container. Patch the runtime everywhere, run only trusted images, and use user namespaces so that even a successful escape lands as an unprivileged user.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Unfaithful without a hint: rationalization on natural prompts
md: Reversed question pairs detect unfaithfulness without planting anything: a consistent reasoner cannot answer Yes to both. This is behavioral evidence, necessary but not sufficient for faithful internal computation, and it shows frontier models rationalize rarely but measurably.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
md: Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
md: Any secret that influences control flow, memory addresses or loop lengths can leak through time, over a network or from another process. Use library functions built to be constant time, keep crypto libraries and firmware patched, and never write your own comparison or scalar multiplication.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: Ask three questions every time: is it legal (law), is it authorised (the owner, in writing, in scope), is it right (harm to others). Keep evidence of each answer before you start.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Testing a system abroad from home does not put you under only your own country's law. Both CMA section 5 and CyBOK's analysis point the same way: the target's location can be enough.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Login banners are not magic. They support consent and notice, but they do not authorise intercepting people who never saw them (a visitor on guest Wi-Fi, the other party to an email), and they do not override necessity and retention limits.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Every lesson's cases share one pattern: the person in trouble had a story that made sense to them ('it was public', 'they agreed afterwards', 'it's only code', 'nothing was merged'). The checklist exists because your own story is the hardest one to see past.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: A gain from an anneal is not proof that the data would help as much over a full pretraining run, or at a larger scale. Llama 3's math annealing helped the 8B model a lot and the 405B model hardly at all. Use anneals to rank candidate datasets, then confirm at the scale you care about.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Vectorizing means rewriting a scalar loop, which handles one element per instruction, into SIMD instructions that handle 8 at once, and compilers can do it automatically. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Collect only what the purpose needs, give every record type a retention period and a trigger, enforce it with a job (not a policy document), and make legal holds the only thing that stops the job.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
md: Insiders already have access, so the programme rests on context (HR events, role), behaviour against the person's own baseline, and exfiltration routes, combined as sequences. Build it with HR, legal and privacy from the start, and pseudonymise until there is cause.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
md: A hosted token service sees your alerts: the alert, including the triggering address, goes to whoever runs the token server. For sensitive placements, run your own. Thinkst publishes the Canarytokens server as open source and recommends its Docker image for self-hosting.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: Three edits turn a GPT into a masked diffusion LM: a [MASK] id, `is_causal=False`, and targets at the same positions as the inputs. In practice add a fourth, relative positions such as RoPE, so the bidirectional model learns locality quickly. At equal size and steps it trains to a worse likelihood than the GPT, and its samples get better as each pass commits fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
md: Scaling or admitting on the current load of the other pool oscillates. Mooncake saw it with early rejection: decode looks idle, so many requests are admitted; they reach decode one prefill later, decode looks full, so admissions stop and prefill idles, and the cycle repeats in opposite phase. Its fix was to decide on the decode load predicted for when the request will arrive there.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH's fine print: signed prekeys, replay, deniability, misbinding
md: Verify every signature on a bundle before any DH, abort on failure, delete one-time prekey private keys after use, rotate signed prekeys, rate-limit bundle fetches, and make the session's next key depend on fresh randomness from Bob.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Metadata: sealed sender and the statistics that undo it
md: Hiding a field is not hiding a pattern. Any metadata defence must be judged over many messages and against an observer who sees timing, sizes and automatic replies, not one message at a time.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Operational failures: Signalgate and the TeleMessage archive (2025)
md: E2EE protects the channel between ends. It cannot decide who the ends are (group membership), what an end does with plaintext (archiving clients, screenshots, backups), or whether that channel is the right one for the information (classification and records policy).

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Estimate cost as event rate x cost per event. Keep the rate low (stable, specific probes; filters; sampling) and keep the work in the kernel (maps, not printf). That is what makes bpftrace usable on a live production system.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Pulse Secure and FortiOS, 2019: file reads that leaked passwords
md: Patching closes the hole. It does not un-leak what already leaked. After any file-read bug on an edge device, rotate every secret the device held and every password typed through it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Responding to a compromised appliance: evidence, rebuild, rotate
md: Evidence first, then the fix. Collect what the vendor's procedure allows before patching or rebooting, isolate without powering off once compromise is found, patch, and if compromise is possible rebuild and rotate every secret the device held or saw.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from
md: Misconception: "the filter should just decode more". A filter in front of an application cannot know how many decoding or normalising steps come later, or in what order. Make the component that acts on the value own the check, and treat upstream filters as an extra layer, not the defence.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Canonical identifiers and idempotence: the Spotify takeover
md: Test canonicalisation functions for idempotence (`f(f(x)) == f(x)`) on every input you accept, and refuse inputs that fail. Store and compare only the canonical form; never re-canonicalise an already-canonical value and expect it to stay put unless that property is enforced.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise
md: Two questions catch most bugs in this course: "Is this check running on the exact value that will be used?" and "Is anything else going to parse these bytes?"

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
md: Allowlisting answers "should this code run at all?", a question EDR never asks. Start in audit, read every 3076, block LOLBins you do not need, keep the driver blocklist on, and then treat every 3077 as a signal.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
md: Event-based NILM reads each step as one appliance switching. When two appliances switch inside one sample, the switch continuity assumption breaks: the net step looks like a third, unrelated appliance, and the ON/OFF bookkeeping fails for both. Higher sample rates make such coincidences rarer but never impossible.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: Each field adds $\log_2(m/u)$. Agreement on a rare value (a domain) is worth far more than agreement on a common one (a city), and a missing field adds nothing instead of counting as a disagreement.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Companies and schools: registries, hierarchies, renames and acronyms
md: Never fuzzy-match short acronyms. Jaro-Winkler rewards shared prefixes, so `ucl` scores 0.94 against `ucla`. Match acronyms exactly against an alias table, and treat any acronym with more than one entity as ambiguous until another field decides.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
md: An app is defined once (application object, home tenant) and instantiated per tenant (service principal). Credentials live with the definition, permissions with the instance. Anyone who can add a credential to a powerful app becomes that app.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
md: In device code flow, the tokens go to whoever started the flow, not to whoever signed in. Block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy except where a known device needs it, and hunt for deviceCode in sign-in logs followed by device registrations.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
md: Every component that bridges AD to Entra ID (the sync server and its accounts, PTA agents, the AZUREADSSOACC key, AD FS) can create or impersonate cloud identities. Treat each as Tier 0, roll the Seamless SSO key at least every 30 days, and keep cloud admins cloud-only.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: ASLR and PIE: moving the targets on every run
md: Common misconception: "ASLR makes the overflow fail." It does not stop the corruption at all; the attacker still overwrites the pointer. ASLR only makes the *value* they write likely to be wrong. Anything that tells them the right value (next lesson) cancels it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
md: Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers (queues that hold a core's writes while it keeps running) and out-of-order execution (running later independent instructions while an earlier one waits), prefetch lines before they are asked for, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
md: A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
md: ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving
md: MoE cost is not just FLOPs. Every layer adds two all-to-alls that must be overlapped with compute, small experts need many tokens per step to stop being memory-bound, and serving must keep all experts resident and batch widely enough that reading their weights is shared by many tokens.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records
md: Misconception: "The TPM checks the boot." It does not decide anything. It only stores what firmware and loaders tell it. Enforcement comes from Secure Boot, from sealing, or from a remote verifier reading the values (lesson 11).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit
md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: MLA in FlashInfer: attention over a compressed latent cache
md: A classic bug: setting `sm_scale` to $1/\sqrt{576}$ because the kernel's dot products are 576 wide. Absorption only regroups the original product $q^C \cdot k^C + q^R \cdot k^R$, whose head dimension was $128 + 64 = 192$, so the scale stays $1/\sqrt{192}$. FlashInfer's own test comments it as the head dimension before matrix absorption.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: The Dolev-Yao intruder: owns the network, not the mathematics
md: "Perfect cryptography" is a modelling assumption, not a claim about real algorithms. A symbolic proof says: if the primitives behave like these equations, the protocol logic is sound. It says nothing about weak parameters, nonce collisions or timing leaks. Those need the computational model or code-level verification, covered later.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Model checking a distributed security protocol with TLA+
md: The model is small on purpose: two replicas, one token, no message loss or duplication. A real design review would add those environment actions (the Formal verification of systems code course shows how) and a liveness property (the revocation eventually completes). A passing check is only as strong as the environment you allowed.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
md: Refinement says nothing about the steps the mapping hides. If the mapping ignores a variable that matters (say, durable state on disk), a wrong design can still refine the spec. Review the mapping as carefully as the spec.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: "FP8 training" does not mean every tensor is FP8. In the FP8 paper, DeepSeek-V3 and the NVFP4 report alike, only the *inputs* to GEMMs are FP8. GEMM outputs come out in BF16 or FP32, and normalizations, softmax, the master weights and optimizer state stay in higher precision. Lesson 4 shows what that means for memory and speed, and the recipes that push FP8 into communication and optimizer state too.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a fake quantizer for E4M3, MXFP4 and NVFP4
md: A fake quantizer reproduces a format's numerics, not its speed: what each value becomes after casting and scaling. Real hardware adds its own accumulation precision and order, so validate surprising results on the target GPU, but use the fake quantizer to test a recipe on your own tensors first.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Network and device signals: IPs, proxies and fingerprints
md: Single signals are weak: IPs can be rented, fingerprints spoofed. Value comes from combining them and from relationships: the same device across many accounts, or claims that contradict each other.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
md: Never log, store or send card numbers through your own analytics, logs or support tools to "help fraud analysis". Work with your provider's card fingerprint instead: it links repeat use of a card without bringing the card data into PCI DSS scope.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
md: "Fraud went down" can mean the control worked, the attackers moved elsewhere, or labels have not arrived yet. Always read loss together with friction (approval rate, insult rate) and with label maturity.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
md: A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Choose the structure by the job. A search engine field: Elasticsearch or Lucene `fuzzy` with `AUTO`. A database column: `pg_trgm` with a GIN or GiST index, then rerank. Single-word spelling correction against a fixed dictionary: SymSpell or a Levenshtein automaton. Matching names or records: lesson 9 builds that pipeline end to end.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
md: A trip runs on date D if its service_id is active on service day D. Its times are offsets from noon minus 12 hours on D, may exceed 24:00:00, and are in agency_timezone. Anything you compute from the schedule must keep the pair (trip_id, service date), not just trip_id.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: A 75-cent gap and the Morris worm: the 1980s internet learns
md: 1980s lessons that still hold: reconcile records that should agree; plant decoys that only an intruder would touch; and when something spreads, close the entry points rather than chasing copies. The worm also produced an institution, CERT/CC, which is why there is now a neutral place to report vulnerabilities.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: 2010: Operation Aurora and Stuxnet bring state operations into view
md: "It came from a nation state, so nothing could have stopped it" is a common excuse. Aurora still needed an unpatched browser and a flat internal network; Stuxnet most likely relied on removable media to reach isolated engineering computers. Sophisticated attackers raise the bar for detection, but basic controls still remove paths.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: MOVEit and xz: mass extortion and the backdoor that almost shipped
md: "Open source is safe because many eyes review it" did not hold: the trigger was only in release tarballs, which few people compare against git, and the payload hid in binary test files. It was caught by one engineer chasing a performance anomaly, not by review.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: Misconception: "adding a random delay hides the timing". Noise only forces the attacker to average more measurements; Paul Kocher showed in 1996 that the number of measurements grows with the square of the noise (lesson 2). Remove the dependency instead.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Where an HTTP/1.1 message ends: Content-Length and chunked
md: Python's own number parsing is lenient: `int('0x5', 16)` and `int('+5')` both return 5, and `int('1_0', 16)` returns 16 because underscores are allowed. That is why the parser checks that a chunk size contains only hex digits and Content-Length only decimal digits **before** converting. Two servers that both "parse numbers" can still disagree about which strings are numbers.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Poisoning with errors and with normalisation
md: Cache and origin must agree on two things: which requests are errors, and which URLs are the same resource. Make the cache stricter than the origin on input, and make its key normalisation match how the origin routes.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: The synchronous stall is the classic THP latency spike. `/proc/vmstat` counts it: `compact_stall` increments every time a process stalls to run compaction, with `compact_success` and `compact_fail` alongside. A rising `compact_stall` next to tail-latency spikes is a strong hint. Tail latency is the time of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile, called p99.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
md: A recurrent state is compact but not divisible. Every serving feature that cuts a cache at an arbitrary token (sharing a prefix, rejecting speculative tokens, pausing a prefill) needs a saved state at that exact position or a recomputation from an earlier one. Plan where states are checkpointed the way you plan KV memory.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: When fusion hurts, and weighting per query
md: Fusion is not free. Before fusing, measure each retriever alone on your queries. If one is far weaker, equal-weight RRF can lower early precision; down-weight it, tune alpha, or drop it.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Misconception: SSO means one session. It means one *login*. After it, the IdP has a session and every app has its own, with its own cookie and lifetime. Disabling a user at the IdP does not end the app sessions already issued (lesson 10).

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
md: Offboarding gap: disabling a user at the IdP stops new logins, not existing app sessions or refresh tokens. A complete offboarding or account-takeover response also ends sessions in each app: through back-channel logout or signals where supported, through the app's admin API or SCIM deactivation (next lesson) where not.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
md: A break-glass account that nobody monitors is just a permanent, policy-exempt Global Administrator. Its safety comes entirely from being rare, strongly authenticated, loudly alerted and regularly tested.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Signed updates and anti-rollback: what a device must check
md: Fuses are a scarce, permanent budget. Bump the rollback version only when an old image has a security bug worth blocking, as MCUboot's separate security counter allows. Burn the bit only after the new image has proved it works (lesson 10), or a bad update could leave the device unable to boot anything.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
md: In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: The vulnerable driver blocklist: what it holds and how to deploy it
md: The blocklist uses **Authenticode** hashes, which skip the signature and checksum fields of the file. Sysmon, most EDRs and threat-intel feeds use **flat file** hashes (SHA-256 of every byte). The two do not match for the same signed driver. Build each list with the hash type its consumer computes.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
md: Treat distillation as function matching: same input to teacher and student every step, as many distinct inputs as you can generate, and a schedule far longer than supervised training. Judge the run against a same-size model trained on labels, and track agreement with the teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction scores are not free under fused attention. A method that needs every step's attention weights (H2O) needs eager attention, a second pass or a custom kernel. A method that scores once after prefill (SnapKV) leaves the decode kernel unchanged. With GQA, combine the scores over each group before choosing.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
md: Question-aware compression works when the scoring queries are the question. Question-agnostic compression has to guess, and eviction cannot undo a wrong guess. Measure accuracy by needle depth, not only on average.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Vector clocks: detecting concurrency exactly
md: Lamport clocks give one-way causality in one integer. Vector clocks give exact causality and detect concurrency, at the cost of one integer per node in every timestamp and every message.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term
md: Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
md: In production, LambdaMART is the training objective of a tree ensemble that rescores the top candidates of a first-stage retriever. Its quality depends on labels (judgments or debiased clicks), query-grouped data, and a truncation level that matches the positions users see.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: One family, many transitions: RetNet to GLA, Mamba2, RWKV-7, KDA
md: To place a new linear-attention layer, ask two questions. What is $A_t$: identity, scalar, diagonal, identity minus rank 1, or diagonal plus low rank? And what does the write minimize: a dot-product reward (additive) or a regression error (delta)? Richer $A_t$ means finer forgetting and a costlier kernel.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look
md: Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring a service sandbox with systemd-analyze security
md: `systemd-analyze security` turns sandboxing into a number you can track per unit and gate in CI with `--offline=yes --threshold=`. Lower is better, but the score covers only systemd's own settings and cannot tell you what the service legitimately needs.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Falco: turning the system call stream into alerts
md: Falco = driver (modern eBPF by default) + state + YAML rules (condition, output, priority, macros, lists). It detects, it does not block. Every exclusion you add is a deliberate blind spot; write it down.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Patching a fleet: automatic updates, restarts, reboots and rings
md: Automate installation (unattended-upgrades, dnf-automatic), automate restarts (needrestart), schedule reboots or livepatch urgent kernel fixes, roll out in rings with canaries, and verify the running version, not the package database.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools (each tool gets only the permissions its job needs), human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Build and run a router in production
